findings.title: 19 Chrome and Edge Extensions Deliver a Wallet Drainer and Credential-Stealing Payloads
findings.summary_md: Socket researchers found 19 malicious extensions published in the last six months, 18 for Chrome and one for Microsoft Edge. The first versions were functional and clean, then later updates delivered a modular framework that opens encrypted WebSocket sessions to command-and-control servers, strips Content Security Policy headers, and executes JavaScript modules served by the attacker. Fourteen extensions were built by the actor and five were bought from legitimate authors; the acquired copy-unlock extension called Enable Right Click and Copy Smart Unlock plus OCR had about 70,000 Chrome users and its Edge counterpart about 10,000 when malicious code appeared. Socket says the Chrome version had been removed but the Edge version was still serving malware at publication time, with a replacement C2 domain introduced on August 14, 2026.

findings.title: 19 Chrome and Edge Extensions Found With Wallet-Stealing and Crypto-Draining Code
findings.summary_md: The Hacker News reported Socket's Superior campaign and listed the extension IDs, including the acquired Chrome copy-unlock tool and its Edge twin. The report notes evidence that the activity may date to February 2024 and that QuickLens had already been flagged earlier in 2026 by Annex Security and monxresearch-sec for pushing malware, injecting arbitrary code, and harvesting data. It describes wallet secret theft, crypto draining, credential theft, browser-history exfiltration, and fake browser-update ClickFix lures across the 19 extensions.

findings.title: Chrome Extension Turns Malicious After Ownership Transfer, Enabling Code Injection and Data Theft
findings.summary_md: The Hacker News covered Chrome extensions QuickLens, with about 7,000 users, and ShotBird, with about 800, after ownership transfers turned them malicious. QuickLens was listed for sale on October 11, 2025, changed owner on February 1, 2026, and received a malicious update on February 17, 2026 that stripped security headers and polled a server every five minutes for JavaScript stored in local storage. The injected code ran through a hidden image element, delivered ClickFix update prompts that led to a Windows PowerShell chain and googleupdate.exe, and captured form data, passwords, browsing history, and tokens.

findings.title: 100+ Fake Chrome Extensions Found Hijacking Sessions, Stealing Credentials, Injecting Ads
findings.summary_md: The Hacker News reported DomainTools research describing more than 100 fake websites and malicious Chrome extensions from an actor active since approximately February 2024. The add-ons appeared to work as advertised while sending data to attacker servers, receiving commands, and executing arbitrary code, with manifest.json permissions spanning every visited site. DomainTools observed an onreset handler on a temporary document object model element used to bypass Content Security Policy, WebSocket connections for proxying traffic, and impersonation of services including DeepSeek, Manus, DeBank, FortiVPN, and Site Stats.
